help.tips[0].examples[0].en: I see the train that is just leaving.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: The cake you baked is great.
help.tips[0].check.whyEn: Inside the relative clause the technician does the repairing, so he is the subject: der, even though the main clause has den Techniker.
help.tips[0].en.text: Ich kenne den Mann, der dort steht (he stands → Nom). Der Mann, den ich kenne, wohnt hier (I know him → Akk). The noun's case in the main sentence is irrelevant.
help.tips[0].en.title: Case from inside the clause, never from outside
help.tips[0].en.trap: English 'that' does not change, so learners copy the main-clause case. Ask only: inside the relative clause, is it doing the verb (der) or receiving it (den)?
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: The phone I bought yesterday doesn't work.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: The colleague who sits next to me is from Vienna.
help.tips[1].check.whyEn: A relative clause in the middle has a comma on both sides and its verb at the end; the main verb kommt follows straight after the second comma.
help.tips[1].en.text: Die Frau, | die Deutsch spricht, | ist nett. Der Film, | den wir sehen wollen, | läuft um acht. Close the relative clause with its verb, then continue the main clause immediately with its verb.
help.tips[1].en.title: The clause in the middle: two commas, main verb waits
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: Those are the people I'd like to invite to the party.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: That is the film we have wanted to see for a long time.
help.tips[2].check.whyEn: In the relative clause the conjugated modal goes last, after the infinitive: die wir mieten wollen.
help.tips[2].en.text: …, das ich gekauft habe · …, den wir sehen wollen · …, die ich einladen möchte. The relative clause is a subordinate clause; everything obeys the verb-last rule.
help.tips[2].en.title: Perfekt and modals inside: helper last
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: the city I love — the cities I know
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: the train that leaves — the train I take
help.tips[3].check.whyEn: Only the masculine changes in the accusative (den); neuter stays das: das Buch, das ich lese.
help.tips[3].en.text: der die das die / den die das die. Say it as a rhythm. Dative and genitive relatives (dem, denen, dessen) are the next quiz.
help.tips[3].en.title: Nom = article, Akk = article except den
help.context.en: The colleague who sits next to me is from Vienna. The project we're doing right now is difficult, but the boss who leads it is very experienced. The customers we're meeting tomorrow have lots of questions. And the coffee our machine makes is the best in the company.
help.mistakes[0].whyEn: Inside the clause he is the subject: der.
help.mistakes[1].whyEn: A middle relative clause needs a closing comma.
help.hookEn: Describe people and things in one flowing sentence – der Kollege, der neben mir sitzt – even with the clause in the middle.
help.introEn: The relative clause you already know, consolidated and stretched. The pronoun is still der, die, das, die by gender and number; nominative when it is the subject of its clause, accusative (den) when it is the object; comma before, verb at the end. What is new here is where the clause can sit and what can be inside it. It can interrupt the main sentence: Die Frau, die Deutsch spricht, ist nett — two commas, and the main verb waits until the clause is closed. It can contain a Perfekt or a modal: das Handy, das ich gestern gekauft habe; der Film, den wir sehen wollen. And the relative pronoun is chosen only by its role inside its own clause, never by the noun's role outside it: Ich kenne den Mann, der dort steht — den in the main clause, der in the relative clause, because there he is the subject.
help.rememberEn[0]: Choose der/den by the pronoun's job inside its clause.
help.rememberEn[1]: Middle clause = two commas, and the main verb comes right after the second.
help.recallEn.known: From "Relativsätze: der, die, das (Nom/Akk)": the pronoun is the article, only den is new.
help.recallEn.today: The clause in the middle of a sentence, and Perfekt or a modal inside it.
sentences[0].whyEn: In the relative clause the man is the subject of steht: der.
sentences[1].whyEn: ich is the subject, the man is kennen's object: accusative den.
sentences[3].whyEn: Object of lesen, a das-word: das — unchanged in the accusative.
sentences[5].whyEn: Object of bestellen, feminine: die — feminine doesn't show the accusative.
sentences[6].whyEn: Object of sehen, masculine: den — only masculine shows the difference.
sentences[16].whyEn: The laptop is what was given — accusative: den; mir is the dative.
sentences[17].whyEn: The doctor is what was recommended — accusative masculine: den.
